subChunks.title: Advanced Quantum Mechanics
subChunks.hookHtml:
“Quantum mechanics,” Theodora said, setting down a copy of Dirac’s Principles of Quantum Mechanics, “is the most precisely tested theory in the history of science. Its prediction of the electron’s magnetic moment agrees with experiment to eleven decimal places — the equivalent of measuring the distance from London to New York to within a millimetre. And yet, after a century of unbroken experimental success, nobody fully agrees on what it means.”

At the Junior level, you encountered the conceptual foundations: wave-particle duality, the uncertainty principle, the probabilistic interpretation of the wave function. Now we go deeper. Advanced quantum mechanics means working with the Schrödinger equation, understanding quantum states as vectors in Hilbert space, mastering the formalism of operators and eigenvalues, and grappling seriously with what measurements do to quantum systems. It also means examining interpretations critically — Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, pilot wave — not as philosophical curiosities but as genuinely different accounts of physical reality that currently make identical experimental predictions.

Theodora opened the book to the first page. “Dirac wrote that this is not a book about physics. It is a book about the mathematics that underlies physics. In quantum mechanics more than anywhere, the mathematics is not just a tool — it is the thing itself.”
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Schrödinger Equation

The time-dependent Schrödinger equation governs how quantum states evolve:

iℏ ∂Ψ/∂t = ĤΨ

where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, Ψ is the wave function (a complex-valued field), and Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator (total energy operator). For a particle in a potential V(x):

Ĥ = −(ℏ²/2m)(∂²/∂x²) + V(x)

For time-independent potentials, separation of variables gives the time-independent Schrödinger equation: ĤΨ = EΨ — an eigenvalue equation where E are the allowed energies and Ψ are the corresponding stationary states.

The Hilbert Space Formalism

Quantum states are vectors in a complex Hilbert space. In Dirac notation (bra-ket notation): a state is written as |ψ⟩ (a “ket”), its dual as ⟨ψ| (a “bra”), and inner products as ⟨φ|ψ⟩ (a complex number giving the overlap between states). Probabilities are |⟨φ|ψ⟩|².

Observables correspond to Hermitian operators — operators whose eigenvalues are real (since measured quantities must be real numbers). Measuring an observable gives one of its eigenvalues. The state collapses to the corresponding eigenstate. Between measurements, the system evolves deterministically via the Schrödinger equation. This measurement postulate is one of the most contentious aspects of quantum mechanics.

Superposition: Any state can be written as a linear combination of eigenstates: |ψ⟩ = Σ cₙ|n⟩. The probability of finding eigenvalue Eₙ on measurement is |cₙ|². The expectation value (average outcome over many measurements) is ⟨Ĥ⟩ = ⟨ψ|Ĥ|ψ⟩.

The Particle in a Box — Quantisation

The simplest non-trivial solution: a particle confined between x=0 and x=L with infinite potential walls. The boundary conditions (Ψ=0 at walls) restrict solutions to standing waves:

Ψₙ(x) = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), n = 1, 2, 3, ...

Corresponding energies: Eₙ = n²π²ℏ²/(2mL²) = n²E₁

The energy is quantised — only discrete values are allowed, with n the quantum number. The ground state (n=1) has energy E₁ > 0 — zero-point energy, a direct consequence of the uncertainty principle (a particle with zero energy would have precisely zero momentum and precisely confined position, violating Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2). This zero-point energy has measurable physical consequences, including the Casimir effect (attractive force between uncharged conducting plates due to vacuum fluctuations).

The Hydrogen Atom

Solving the Schrödinger equation for the Coulomb potential (V = −e²/4πε₀r) gives the hydrogen energy levels:

Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV (n = 1, 2, 3, ...)

The full solution requires three quantum numbers: principal n (energy), angular momentum l (0 to n−1), and magnetic mₗ (−l to +l). Including electron spin (s = ±1/2), four quantum numbers specify each electron state. The Pauli Exclusion Principle (no two fermions in the same quantum state) and these quantum numbers together explain the structure of the periodic table.

The wave functions (orbitals) are probability density distributions. The 1s orbital is spherically symmetric. p-orbitals have two lobes along an axis. The shapes arise directly from the mathematics — they are not artistic choices but solutions to a partial differential equation.

Entanglement

Two particles can exist in entangled states where the quantum state of the pair cannot be factored into individual particle states. For a two-particle system in the Bell state |Φ⁺⟩ = (1/√2)(|↑↑⟩ + |↓↓⟩), measuring particle A’s spin instantly determines what you will find if you measure particle B’s spin, regardless of separation distance. This is not hidden information — John Bell proved in 1964 that no “hidden variable” theory can reproduce quantum mechanics’ predictions without faster-than-light connections. Bell inequality experiments (Aspect 1982; Hensen et al. 2015 with no loopholes closed) confirm quantum mechanics and rule out local hidden variable theories. Crucially, entanglement cannot be used to transmit information faster than light — the no-communication theorem.

Interpretations of Quantum Mechanics

The formalism is agreed upon; its interpretation is not:

Copenhagen interpretation: Wave function collapse is real and occurs upon measurement. The wave function represents knowledge, not objective reality. Questions about what happens between measurements are meaningless. Most physicists use this in practice — it is pragmatic and does not commit to ontological claims.

Many-Worlds (Everett): The wave function never collapses. Every quantum measurement causes the universe to branch, with all outcomes occurring in different branches. No collapse; no special role for observers. All branches are equally real. Problems: the preferred basis problem (what defines “branches”?), and explaining the Born rule (why |cₙ|² gives probabilities).

Pilot wave (de Broglie-Bohm): Particles have definite positions at all times, guided by a real wave field. Deterministic, but non-local — the wave function encodes all particle correlations globally. Recovers all quantum predictions. Problems: extending to relativistic quantum field theory is technically difficult.

QBism: Quantum states represent an agent’s personal beliefs about measurement outcomes — explicitly a tool for prediction, not a picture of objective reality.

All interpretations agree on experimental predictions. The choice between them is currently empirically underdetermined — a genuine open problem at the intersection of physics and philosophy of science.

Quantum Technologies — Where Advanced QM Becomes Engineering

Quantum mechanics underpins growing technological applications: quantum computing (qubits in superposition exploit quantum parallelism; Shor’s algorithm factors large numbers exponentially faster than classical algorithms, threatening RSA encryption); quantum cryptography (BB84 protocol uses quantum no-cloning theorem to guarantee secure key distribution — any eavesdropper necessarily disturbs the signal); quantum sensing (atomic clocks accurate to 1 second in 15 billion years; quantum magnetometers for brain imaging); and quantum simulation (using controllable quantum systems to model other quantum systems — useful for drug discovery and material science).

storyBeats.text: Theodora wrote the Schrödinger equation on the board and stood back. “This is the fundamental law of quantum mechanics. It is completely deterministic — given the state now, it predicts the state at any future time with perfect precision. So where does the randomness come from?”
“From measurement? When you actually look at a particle, the wave function collapses to a definite value — and that’s the random step?”

“According to Copenhagen, yes. But notice what that requires: a sharp distinction between ‘quantum system’ and ‘classical observer.’ Measurement happens at the boundary. Everett asked: what if there is no boundary? What if the observer is also quantum? Then both outcomes happen — in different branches of a superposition. The randomness becomes the apparent experience of a single branch.”
“And de Broglie-Bohm says particles always have definite positions — we just can’t know them because the guiding wave is nonlocal. All three agree on every experiment?”

“By design, yes. Bell’s theorem rules out local hidden variables. But non-local hidden variables like Bohm’s are still possible. The interpretations are empirically equivalent but ontologically radical — they describe completely different realities. We cannot choose between them by experiment. That is a genuinely uncomfortable position for a science that prides itself on empirical testability.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain quantum entanglement to a 16-year-old. Make clear what makes it strange, what it does not allow (sending information faster than light), and how Bell’s experiment proved that Einstein’s ‘hidden variables’ explanation cannot work.
learningObjectives: Interpret the time-independent Schrödinger equation as an eigenvalue problem and apply it to the particle-in-a-box model to derive quantised energy levels
Use Dirac bra-ket notation to represent quantum states, calculate inner products, and determine measurement probabilities from expansion coefficients
Explain quantum entanglement, Bell’s theorem, and the experimental evidence ruling out local hidden variable theories
Compare and critically evaluate at least three interpretations of quantum mechanics, identifying what empirical evidence can and cannot decide between them
commonMistakes: Treating wave function collapse as a physical process with a mechanism — the collapse is a feature of the measurement postulate, not something QM explains; it is what different interpretations dispute
Thinking entanglement allows faster-than-light communication — the no-communication theorem strictly prevents this; correlations are only apparent when classical information is compared
Confusing the uncertainty principle with measurement disturbance — ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2 is a statement about the intrinsic spread of values in quantum states, not just observer disturbance

Believing the Many-Worlds interpretation is obviously correct because it avoids collapse — it faces serious problems (preferred basis, Born rule derivation) and is not experimentally confirmed over alternatives
assessmentCriteria: Can apply the particle-in-a-box model quantitatively: write wave functions, calculate energy levels, and interpret the zero-point energy result
Can describe Bell’s theorem and explain what the Aspect-type experiments demonstrate about local hidden variables — distinguishing what is and is not proven
Can compare the Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, and pilot wave interpretations in terms of their ontological commitments and the arguments for and against each
Can identify at least two quantum technologies and explain which quantum mechanical principle (superposition, entanglement, no-cloning) each exploits
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
An electron is confined in a one-dimensional infinite potential well of width L = 0.50 nm (roughly the diameter of an atom).

  1. Write the formula for the energy of the nth quantum state. Use ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and mₑ = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
  2. Calculate E₁, the ground state energy, in eV (1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).
  3. Calculate E₂ and E₃. What is the pattern?
  4. If the electron transitions from the n=3 to n=1 state, what is the energy of the photon emitted? In what part of the electromagnetic spectrum does this photon lie?
  5. Why can the electron not have zero energy? Connect your answer to the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Energy formula:
Eₙ = n²π²ℏ²/(2mₑL²)

2. Ground state energy E₁:
E₁ = π²(1.055 × 10⁻³⁴)² / (2 × 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × (0.50 × 10⁻⁹)²)
= π² × 1.113 × 10⁻⁶⁸ / (2 × 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁹)
= 1.097 × 10⁻⁶⁷ / 4.555 × 10⁻⁴⁹
= 2.41 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
= 2.41 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.50 eV

3. E₂ and E₃:
E₂ = 4E₁ = 6.02 eV
E₃ = 9E₁ = 13.57 eV
Pattern: Eₙ = n²E₁ — energies scale as the square of the quantum number.

4. Photon from n=3 → n=1:
ΔE = E₃ − E₁ = 13.57 − 1.50 = 12.07 eV
This is in the ultraviolet range. (Visible is ~1.8–3.1 eV; UV begins above ~3.1 eV.)
λ = hc/ΔE = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / (12.07 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 103 nm — UV.

5. Zero energy and the Uncertainty Principle:
If the electron had zero energy (E=0), it would have zero momentum (p=0, so Δp=0). But it is confined within the well (Δx ≤ L). The Uncertainty Principle requires Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2, so Δp ≥ ℏ/(2L) > 0 — the momentum cannot be zero. A non-zero momentum corresponds to non-zero kinetic energy, which is E₁. The ground state zero-point energy is not just a mathematical artefact; it is a direct consequence of confinement and the uncertainty principle.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Richard Feynman famously said, “If you think you understand quantum mechanics, you don’t understand quantum mechanics.” Evaluate this claim. In your response: (a) identify what makes quantum mechanics genuinely difficult to interpret (beyond the mathematics); (b) assess whether the interpretational disagreements among physicists reflect a failure of understanding or a genuine limitation of the current theoretical framework; (c) consider whether a theory can be complete as a predictive framework while remaining incomplete as a description of reality; and (d) discuss whether the development of quantum technologies (computing, cryptography) settles or bypasses these interpretational debates.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) What makes QM genuinely difficult to interpret:
The mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics is clear and unambiguous — the Schrödinger equation, the Born rule, operator methods. The difficulty is ontological: what does the wave function represent? If it represents objective reality, then superpositions of “cat alive” and “cat dead” are real — but we never observe such superpositions in everyday life. If it represents our knowledge, then physical reality is observer-dependent, which seems strange for a supposedly universal physical theory. The measurement problem — why unique outcomes emerge from superpositions when we observe — has no agreed solution. These are not mathematical difficulties but questions about what the mathematics refers to in the world.

(b) Interpretational disagreements — failure or limitation?
The disagreements reflect a genuine limitation of the framework. All major interpretations reproduce quantum mechanical predictions identically — they are empirically equivalent. Bell’s theorem rules out local hidden variables, but non-local hidden variables (Bohmian mechanics) remain viable. Without new experimental predictions that distinguish them, the choice is currently underdetermined by evidence. This is not physicists failing to understand the equations; it is a failure of the equations to uniquely determine their own ontological content. Some philosophers of physics argue this is unprecedented in science — a theory with no agreed interpretation after a century of use.

(c) Predictively complete but ontologically incomplete:
Yes, this is precisely the situation. “Shut up and calculate” (often attributed to Feynman or Mermin) is a coherent pragmatic stance: quantum mechanics is used to make predictions with extraordinary accuracy. No experiment requires an interpretation to design or interpret. From a strict instrumentalist philosophy of science, a theory that predicts all observable results is complete. From a realist perspective — where science aims to describe how things actually are, not just predict measurements — QM is radically incomplete. Both positions are philosophically defensible; the tension between them is the source of the ongoing debate.

(d) Do quantum technologies settle interpretational debates?
No — and this is a revealing point. Quantum computers exploit superposition and entanglement to speed up certain computations. Quantum cryptography exploits the no-cloning theorem. These work because the formal rules of QM (superposition, entanglement, Born rule) are followed correctly — they are agnostic about interpretation. A Many-Worlds believer, a Copenhagen adherent, and a Bohmian all design the same quantum circuit. The technologies demonstrate that the formalism is correct and useful; they do not tell us what the formalism means. Feynman’s quip retains its force: you can make the technology work without understanding what you are really doing with quantum reality. That is philosophically peculiar, and it remains unresolved.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A thought experiment exposing the measurement problem: if a physicist (Wigner’s friend) measures a quantum system inside an isolated lab, does the wave function collapse for the friend but remain in superposition for an outside observer? Recent experimental tests of extended Wigner’s friend scenarios have found results inconsistent with certain combinations of realist assumptions.

The process by which quantum superpositions are destroyed through interaction with the environment — entanglement with an enormous number of environmental degrees of freedom makes quantum interference effectively unobservable at macroscopic scales. Decoherence explains why we do not see Schrödinger’s cat but does not resolve the measurement problem or explain unique outcomes.

The relativistic generalisation of quantum mechanics, combining SR with QM by treating fields (not particles) as fundamental — particles are excitations of underlying fields. QED (quantum electrodynamics) is the QFT of electromagnetism and is the most precisely tested theory in physics.

A fundamental result in quantum information theory stating that it is impossible to create an exact copy of an unknown quantum state — a direct consequence of the linearity of quantum mechanics. This underpins quantum cryptography’s security guarantees.

The counterintuitive phenomenon whereby a quantum system’s evolution can be slowed or frozen by frequent measurement — the system is repeatedly projected back to its initial state before it can evolve significantly. Experimentally observed in atomic transitions and used in some quantum computing error correction schemes.

Richard Feynman’s reformulation of quantum mechanics, in which a particle simultaneously takes all possible paths between two points, each path contributing a phase factor; quantum amplitudes are obtained by summing (integrating) over all paths. Equivalent to Schrödinger’s formulation but natural for extending to quantum field theory.

questions.questionHtml: An electron in a 1D infinite potential well of width L is in the n=2 state. What is its energy expressed in terms of E₁ (the ground state energy)?
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. Eₙ = n²E₁, so E₂ = 4E₁. The energies scale as the square of the quantum number.

questions.questionHtml: A physicist prepares an electron in the quantum state |ψ⟩ = (3/5)|↑⟩ + (4/5)|↓⟩, where |↑⟩ and |↓⟩ are spin-up and spin-down eigenstates. What is the probability of measuring spin-down?
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. The probability is |c↓|² = (4/5)² = 16/25 = 0.64. Note that |c↑|² + |c↓|² = 9/25 + 16/25 = 25/25 = 1, confirming normalisation.

questions.questionHtml: Decoherence is sometimes cited as solving the measurement problem of quantum mechanics. Critically assess this claim.
options: Decoherence explains why macroscopic superpositions are unobservable in practice, but does not explain why a single definite outcome occurs — it converts quantum superpositions into apparent classical mixtures without selecting one branch
Decoherence fully solves the measurement problem by demonstrating that quantum superpositions collapse into definite states through environmental interaction
Decoherence is irrelevant to the measurement problem because it only applies to macroscopic objects, not to quantum systems in isolation
Decoherence is an interpretation-dependent concept that only makes sense within the Many-Worlds framework
questions.correctAnswer: Decoherence explains why macroscopic superpositions are unobservable in practice, but does not explain why a single definite outcome occurs — it converts quantum superpositions into apparent classical mixtures without selecting one branch
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. Decoherence suppresses interference between branches by entangling the system with a vast environment, making superpositions practically indistinguishable from classical probability distributions. But this is still a superposition — all branches remain in the overall quantum state. It explains the appearance of classicality but not the selection of a unique outcome, leaving the measurement problem intact.
